MOE propagation: margins of error

Source: vignettes/theory-moe-propagation.qmd 
library(catchmentACS)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# Force network-free, deterministic builds: no provider/Census calls, no cache.
old_options <- options(
  catchmentACS.progress = "off",
  catchmentACS.rate_first_default = FALSE
)
old_cache <- getOption("catchmentACS.cache_enabled", NULL)
on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
on.exit(options(catchmentACS.cache_enabled = old_cache), add = TRUE)
cacs_set_cache(FALSE, scope = "session")

This article is the method-track companion to vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS") that develops the uncertainty half of the estimator. The overview names the four margin-of-error (MOE) formula families and states the M = 1.645\,SE conversion; this article derives them — the SE/MOE relation, the weighted root-sum-square for sums and means, the two ratio-variance forms, the never-silent C1 → C2 fallback, and the numerical guards — and then does the thing the overview cannot: it reproduces the package’s MOE arithmetic by hand on a bundled fixture and triggers the fallback on purpose, so a methodologist can confirm that the formulas on this page are the formulas the code runs. The reference page ?cacs_propagate_moe is the implementation anchor; this article supplies the mathematics behind its “MOE formula families” section.

It is written for a reader who wants the propagation model on the page: why variances must accumulate on the standard-error scale, why a weighted sum and a weighted mean share one combination rule, why a ratio has two variance formulas and which one is the default, and exactly what the package records when the tighter formula breaks down. We reuse the notation fixed in the overview without re-motivating it: the isochrone I_s, the tract T_j, the coverage weight w^{cov}_{sj} and the normalized mean weight w^{mean}_{sj}, a tract-level count Y_j, a scalar X_j, a ratio’s numerator and denominator counts A_j, B_j, and the published 90% tract margin of error M_j. The spatial half — how those weights are built and how the point estimates \widehat{Y}_s, \widehat{\bar X}_s, \widehat{R}_s aggregate — is derived in vignette("theory-spatial-aggregation", package = "catchmentACS"); this article takes the weights as given and carries the published uncertainty through them.

About the data in this article

Every executable cell here is built entirely from the package’s bundled inst/extdata fixtures — the synthetic legacy_2025_isochrones, legacy_2025_sites, and sample_alabama_subset objects — so this article renders with no Census, OSRM, ORS, or other network calls. These fixtures preserve the production calling contract (sites, drive-time polygons, tract-level ACS variables) but are synthetic and illustrative: they are included only for examples, tests, and reproducible package checks. They are not live Alabama policy estimates and must not be cited as real ACS results. Any real analysis requires a fresh live run (see vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS")).

Why MOE propagation needs its own algebra

Every ACS estimate ships with a published margin of error, and a catchment estimate is a function of many such estimates — a weighted sum of tract counts, a weighted blend of tract scalars, a ratio of two aggregated totals. The published MOEs describe the uncertainty of the inputs; the question this article answers is how that uncertainty travels to the output. Dropping it is not an option: a coverage-weighted count of persons in poverty with no margin of error invites a false precision the underlying survey never claimed. Carrying it naively is just as wrong, because margins of error do not add — a sum of two estimates each with margin M does not have margin 2M.

The propagation rule is the standard one for a linear (or locally linear) combination of approximately independent estimates: variances add, margins of error do not. So the whole apparatus reduces to three moves repeated in four guises — convert each component margin to a variance, combine the variances under the appropriate model, and convert the combined variance back to a margin. The four families differ only in how the variances combine: a weighted sum (Family A), a weighted mean (Family B), a subset proportion (Family C1), and a general ratio (Family C2). The U.S. Census Bureau’s published guidance on approximating the margin of error of derived estimates (its ACS handbook for data users) gives all four; the package reimplements them so the formula, its guards, and its audit trail live in one place.

Two modeling assumptions sit under everything below, and both are inherited from the spatial-aggregation model rather than introduced here. First, the tract-level ACS estimates entering a catchment aggregate are treated as approximately independent, which is what lets their variances add without covariance terms; this is the same assumption the Census Bureau’s own sum-of-estimates approximation makes, and it is generally slightly conservative for positively correlated neighbors. Second, the weights are treated as fixed design quantities, not random — the coverage and mean weights are geometric ratios of measured areas, so they carry no sampling variance of their own. Both are stated plainly so a reader knows exactly what the margins below do and do not capture.

Standard errors, margins of error, and the 90% convention

The U.S. Census Bureau publishes ACS uncertainty as a margin of error (MOE): the half-width of a confidence interval, reported at the 90% level. An estimate \widehat{\theta} ships as \widehat{\theta} \pm M, and the interval [\widehat{\theta} - M,\; \widehat{\theta} + M] is the Bureau’s 90% interval. The MOE is a reported quantity, but it is not the natural quantity for combining uncertainties — variances are. A margin of error and a standard error (SE) are interconvertible through a single confidence multiplier z,

M = z\, SE, \qquad SE = \frac{M}{z},

and at the 90% level the Census multiplier is

z = 1.645, \qquad\text{so}\qquad M = 1.645\, SE, \qquad SE = \frac{M}{1.645}.

The constant 1.645 is the Bureau’s official rounded value of the standard normal 95th percentile; the exact quantile \Phi^{-1}(0.95) \approx 1.6448536 differs only in the fourth decimal place, and the package adopts the rounded 1.645 at the default level so its output is byte-compatible with hand calculations done the Bureau’s way. (The multiplier is configurable through the level argument; any other level resolves z from the exact symmetric two-tailed normal quantile instead. Everything below is at the default z = 1.645.)

Why the SE scale matters. Variances of independent quantities add; margins of error do not. If two independent estimates have margins M_1 and M_2, the margin of their sum is not M_1 + M_2. The correct route is to drop to the SE scale, where variances are additive, combine, and convert back:

M_{\text{sum}} = z\, SE_{\text{sum}} = z \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2} = z \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{M_1}{z}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{M_2}{z}\right)^2}.

Every formula in this article is an instance of that pattern: divide each component MOE by z to a standard error, combine the standard errors (or variances) under an independence assumption, multiply the combined SE back by z. The package exposes the two conversions directly as cacs_se_to_moe() and cacs_moe_to_se() (exact inverses at a given level), and both are NA-safe: a missing input returns NA, never a silent zero. Internally the same constant divides MOEs into variances at the start of each family’s calculation and multiplies back at the end.

# M = 1.645 * SE and its exact inverse, on the same vector. NA passes through.
se  <- c(50, 100, NA)
moe <- cacs_se_to_moe(se, level = 0.90)
c(moe = moe, recovered_se = cacs_moe_to_se(moe, level = 0.90))
         moe1          moe2          moe3 recovered_se1 recovered_se2
        82.25        164.50            NA         50.00        100.00
recovered_se3
           NA

The first SE of 50 becomes a margin of 82.25, the second 100 becomes 164.5, and cacs_moe_to_se() recovers the originals exactly; the NA survives both directions. This round-trip is the backbone of every combination below.

Families A and B: the weighted root-sum-square

The first two families propagate margins through a linear combination of tract estimates, and they share one closed form. They differ only in the weight that multiplies each component margin — and that weight is exactly the one the matching estimand family uses for its point estimate, so the uncertainty travels through the same geometry as the estimate.

Family A — spatial total (weighted sum of counts)

A spatial_total is the coverage-weighted sum of tract counts, \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, Y_j, with the coverage weight derived in the spatial-aggregation article. Each tract contributes w^{cov}_{sj}\, Y_j, an estimate whose standard error is w^{cov}_{sj}\, (M_j / z), because a fixed weight scales an SE linearly. Under approximate independence the variances add, so the variance of the catchment total is the sum of the squared coverage-weighted component SEs, and the margin of error is that combined SE lifted back by z:

M = z \sqrt{\sum_j \left(\frac{w^{cov}_{sj}\, M_j}{z}\right)^2}.

This is a root-sum-square of coverage-weighted component MOEs. Read the structure: each published margin M_j is divided by z to a standard error, scaled by that tract’s coverage weight (the fraction of the tract the catchment captured), squared and summed into a variance, and the result is square-rooted and multiplied by z back to a margin. A tract captured whole (w^{cov}_{sj} = 1) contributes its full margin; a tract clipped to a tenth of its area contributes a tenth of it. The root-sum-square — rather than a plain sum — is the arithmetic statement that independent errors partially cancel: the combined margin grows like the square root of the number of comparable terms, not linearly.

Family B — weighted scalar / proxy mean

A scalar proxy — per-capita income, a median-income proxy — is the normalized-mean-weighted blend \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj}\, X_j, with the mean weights that sum to one within a site and drive-time cell. Because the mean weights are also fixed design quantities, the propagation is structurally identical to Family A; only the weight changes from w^{cov} to w^{mean}:

M = z \sqrt{\sum_j \left(\frac{w^{mean}_{sj}\, M_j}{z}\right)^2}.

The single difference from Family A is the weight. The coverage weight allocates a fraction of each tract’s amount and is unbounded in sum; the mean weight is a share that is pre-normalized to sum to one. So a Family-A margin scales with how much area the catchment captured, while a Family-B margin is a weighted average of component margins on the same per-unit scale as the proxy itself — consistent with the point estimate, which is a convex combination of the tract values. In both families the weight that appears in the margin is the same weight that appears in the point estimate: coverage for a total, normalized mean for a proxy. This is the propagation analogue of the central spatial-aggregation point — a count and an average are aggregated by different weights — and it is why a single root-sum-square form serves both with only the weight swapped. (The implementation carries a raw accumulated variance per component and an explicit weight_basis so the two paths never cross; the per-cell normalization for Family B is the package’s responsibility, documented in ?cacs_intersect_weight. A metadata_only row carries no estimate and therefore no margin.)

The numerical check below verifies Family A by hand against the package on a catchment with genuinely partial coverage, so the weights actually bite.

Families C1 and C2: ratio variance, subset versus conservative

A derived_rate is not linear in its inputs — it is a ratio \widehat{R}_s = A/B of two aggregated coverage totals, where both the numerator total A = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} A_j and the denominator total B = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} B_j are random estimates carrying their own propagated variance from Family A. A ratio has no exact finite-sample variance, so propagation uses the standard first-order (delta-method) linearization, and the package offers the two forms the Census Bureau’s handbook gives. Both are stated on the variance scale; the reported margin is recovered as M = z\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(A/B)} at the end. They differ by exactly one sign, and that sign is the hinge of both their statistical meaning and their numerical behavior.

Family C1 — proportion subset

When the numerator A is a true subset of the denominator B — every person counted in A is also counted in B, as persons in poverty are a subset of the population for whom poverty status is determined — the numerator and denominator errors are positively correlated, and the Bureau’s proportion formula subtracts a cross term to credit that correlation:

\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(A/B) \approx \frac{\mathrm{Var}(A) - (A/B)^2\, \mathrm{Var}(B)}{B^2}.

Subtracting the cross term makes this the tighter (smaller) of the two estimates when it is valid, which is the whole reason to use it: it does not double-count the shared sampling uncertainty the subset relationship guarantees. But the subtraction is also its fragility — the bracketed expression can go negative when the denominator’s scaled variance (A/B)^2\,\mathrm{Var}(B) exceeds the numerator’s \mathrm{Var}(A), in which case its square root is undefined and the formula returns no admissible variance. That edge case is handled in the next section, never silently.

Family C2 — general ratio (conservative)

When the subset relationship is not guaranteed — an arbitrary ratio of two counts, or a derived rate where conservative reproducibility is preferred — the correct general form treats the numerator and denominator as approximately independent and adds the cross term:

\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(A/B) \approx \frac{\mathrm{Var}(A) + (A/B)^2\, \mathrm{Var}(B)}{B^2}.

Note the + sign. Two consequences follow from that single change. First, this variance is always non-negative: a sum of two squared, non-negative terms can never go below zero, so Family C2 always yields an admissible margin. Second, it is the conservative estimate — by adding rather than subtracting the cross term, it never understates the uncertainty, at the cost of being slightly wide when the numerator really is a subset. This is exactly the trade the package makes for its curated derived rates: Family C2 (general_ratio_conservative) is the default, and the tighter Family C1 (proportion_subset) is applied only when a true subset relationship is asserted for a rate eligible for it. Among the five curated rates, the poverty rate and labor-force participation are the subset-eligible ones; the SNAP, SSI, and unemployment rates route to C2 by default. The full per-rate policy is derived in vignette("theory-derived-rates", package = "catchmentACS").

The sign is the entire distinction. A single character — the minus in C1, the plus in C2 — separates the tighter, subset-only formula from the conservative, always-defined one. Whether C1 is allowed to break down gracefully is the subject of the fallback.

The C1 → C2 fallback and the status columns

The two ratio formulas are not independent choices made once at dispatch — they are connected by a guard. When a row is dispatched to Family C1 but its subset variance comes out negative, the package does not return a missing value, a silent C1 number, or a NaN a caller might miss. It recomputes the margin with the always-non-negative Family C2 formula so a defensible value is still produced, and — this is the design commitment — it records the substitution per row rather than hiding it. The fallback is never silent.

cacs_propagate_moe() returns, for every row, both the formula the dispatch asked for and the formula it actually used:

Column Meaning
moe_formula_requested the formula the dispatch resolved for this row (here, proportion_subset)
moe_formula_effective the formula whose value was actually written (after any fallback)
moe_fallback TRUE when the effective formula overrode the request
moe_fallback_reason the cause: negative_variance, zero_denominator, missing_moe, or n/a

For the C1 → C2 case specifically, a row whose subset variance went negative is recorded as

  • moe_formula_requested = "proportion_subset" — the request is preserved,
  • moe_formula_effective = "general_ratio_conservative" — C2 produced the value,
  • moe_fallback = TRUE,
  • moe_fallback_reason = "negative_variance".

A clean C1 row that stayed positive keeps moe_formula_effective = "proportion_subset", moe_fallback = FALSE, and moe_fallback_reason = "n/a", and its requested and effective formulas agree. At the end of a run a single summary reports the total counts by reason, and a run-level provenance attribute records how many rows took each path, so the fallback is auditable in aggregate as well as per row. The point of keeping both requested and effective is that the row reads as a self-documenting audit record: this row asked for the subset formula, its variance went negative, so the conservative formula produced the value. An auditor reading the output five years later can reconstruct exactly which rows took which path without rerunning anything; no information is lost and nothing is repaired behind the analyst’s back.

The same moe_fallback/moe_fallback_reason mechanism also records the two degenerate outcomes that are not formula substitutions but value losses, covered next: a zero denominator and a missing input margin both yield NA with their own reason strings.

Numerical guards

Five guards protect the formulas from the inputs real ACS data presents. They are implemented once, in the package’s MOE helpers, so every family inherits the same behavior, and each leaves a visible trace rather than a silent number.

  • Denominator near zero. Families B and C divide by a weight sum or a denominator estimate. When that divisor is within a small epsilon of zero (the package uses the square root of machine epsilon, about 1.5 \times 10^{-8}), the result is set to NA rather than allowed to explode. For a ratio row this is recorded as moe_fallback_reason = "zero_denominator" — the structural reason an empty or near-empty catchment does not masquerade as a precise rate.
  • Negative variance in a proportion. The Family C1 subtraction can go below zero; this is the trigger for the C1 → C2 fallback of the previous section, recorded as moe_fallback_reason = "negative_variance".
  • Missing-margin propagation. A missing component margin propagates to a missing result rather than being silently treated as zero, preserving ACS suppression as a signal. For a ratio row a missing numerator or denominator margin yields NA with moe_fallback_reason = "missing_moe".
  • Non-negative C2 variance. Because C2 adds rather than subtracts, its bracket is provably \ge 0; it has no negative-variance branch and always yields a real margin. This is what makes C2 a safe fallback target for C1.
  • The multiplier is a fixed constant. At the default 90% level z = 1.645 is the Bureau’s rounded value, not the exact normal quantile; this is a deliberate choice for byte-level reproducibility against ACS-published margins, and the roughly 5 \times 10^{-5} gap to \Phi^{-1}(0.95) is absorbed within the package’s regression tolerance. Other confidence levels resolve z at full precision.

The common thread is that none of these guards repairs silently. A zero denominator, a negative subset variance, and a missing margin each leave a typed trace in moe_fallback_reason and feed the end-of-run summary, so a degenerate input is always distinguishable in the output from a clean computation.

Numerical verification: the formulas match the package

This is the section that earns a methodologist’s trust. We do two checks against the real cacs_propagate_moe(), both offline on bundled fixtures, on a single catchment. First we reproduce a Family A weighted root-sum-square entirely by hand and assert it equals the package’s reported margin to machine precision. Then, on the same catchment, we deliberately construct a derived-rate case whose C1 subset variance is negative and watch the package fall back to C2 — recording moe_fallback = TRUE and moe_fallback_reason = "negative_variance" — and we reproduce the C2 value by hand as well. If the formulas on this page were not the formulas the code runs, either check would fail.

We build the catchment from the fixtures with cacs_intersect_weight(), exactly the shapes pipeline stages 1–2 would have produced. We pick a catchment whose coverage is partial and uneven so the weighted root-sum-square is genuinely exercised: AL_SITE_17 at a 10-minute drive intersects three tracts — one fully enclosed and two clipped to about a ninth of their area.

# These fixtures are exactly the shapes stages 1-2 would have returned, frozen.
iso <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_isochrones.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
acs <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "sample_alabama_subset.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))

site_id    <- "AL_SITE_17"
drive_time <- 10L

iso_one <- iso[
  iso$site_id == site_id & iso$drive_time_min == drive_time, ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# keep_tract_audit exposes the per-tract coverage weights we recompute by hand.
weighted <- cacs_intersect_weight(
  iso_sf           = iso_one,
  acs_sf           = acs,
  weight_method    = "area",
  keep_tract_audit = TRUE,
  verbose          = FALSE
)

propagated <- cacs_propagate_moe(weighted, verbose = FALSE)

Step 1 — reproduce a Family A weighted RSS by hand

Persons in poverty (B17001_002) is a spatial_total, so its margin comes from Family A. The per-tract audit gives the coverage weight w^{cov}_{sj} (area_wt); we join each tract’s published margin M_j from the ACS fixture and assemble the inputs:

VAR <- "B17001_002"

audit <- attr(weighted, "cacs_tract_audit") |>
  transmute(GEOID, w_cov = area_wt)

published <- acs |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(GEOID %in% audit$GEOID, variable == VAR) |>
  select(GEOID, M_j = moe)

hand_A <- audit |>
  left_join(published, by = "GEOID") |>
  arrange(desc(w_cov))

hand_A
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID       w_cov   M_j
  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 01125001001 1       200
2 01127001001 0.113   218
3 01123001001 0.113   152

Now the Family A formula, term by term: scale each published margin by its coverage weight, divide by z, square, sum, square-root, and multiply back by z — M = z\sqrt{\sum_j (w^{cov}_{sj} M_j / z)^2}:

z <- 1.645

per_tract_var <- (hand_A$w_cov * hand_A$M_j / z)^2  # (w * M / z)^2 per tract
hand_moe_A    <- z * sqrt(sum(per_tract_var))       # z * sqrt(sum(...))

list(
  per_tract_var = round(per_tract_var, 4),
  summed_var    = sum(per_tract_var),
  hand_moe_A    = hand_moe_A
)
$per_tract_var
[1] 14781.8294   222.3397   108.0903

$summed_var
[1] 15112.26

$hand_moe_A
[1] 202.223

The fully-enclosed tract dominates the combined variance; the two clipped tracts enter with small coverage weights (about a ninth) and contribute little even though their raw published margins are not small — exactly what the weighted form predicts, since the weight, not the raw margin, governs the contribution. Now the package’s own row for the same variable:

pkg_A <- propagated |>
  filter(variable == VAR) |>
  select(variable, estimate, moe, moe_formula_effective, moe_fallback)

pkg_A
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  variable   estimate   moe moe_formula_effective moe_fallback
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                 <lgl>
1 B17001_002    1237.  202. weighted_sum          FALSE       
c(
  moe_match    = isTRUE(all.equal(hand_moe_A, pkg_A$moe)),
  moe_abs_diff = abs(hand_moe_A - pkg_A$moe)
)
   moe_match moe_abs_diff
           1            0

The package routed this count through moe_formula_effective = "weighted_sum" (Family A) with no fallback, and its reported moe — about 202.2 — equals the hand-computed weighted root-sum-square exactly, with an absolute difference of zero. The margin on this page and the margin in the code are the same arithmetic.

Step 2 — trigger the C1 → C2 fallback

Now the fallback. The poverty rate’s numerator B17001_002 is a true subset of its denominator B17001_001, so it is C1-eligible; we will request the proportion_subset formula. To make the subset variance go negative in a fully controlled way, we take the real catchment and lower the numerator’s accumulated variance well below the denominator’s scaled variance (A/B)^2\,\mathrm{Var}(B) — the configuration that drives C1’s bracket below zero. The aggregation carriers (an attribute of the intersect output) hold each component’s coverage total and accumulated variance; we copy them, shrink the numerator’s variance, and attach a matching carrier and long row for the rate:

carr <- attr(weighted, "cacs_aggregation_carriers")

num_code <- "B17001_002"  # poverty_rate numerator (subset)
den_code <- "B17001_001"  # poverty_rate denominator (universe)

A    <- carr$est_total[carr$variable == num_code]      # numerator total
B    <- carr$est_total[carr$variable == den_code]      # denominator total
VarB <- carr$var_total_raw[carr$variable == den_code]  # denominator variance
p    <- A / B                                          # the proportion A / B

# Force C1's bracket Var(A) - p^2 Var(B) below zero by setting the numerator's
# accumulated variance to a quarter of the denominator's scaled variance.
VarA_neg <- 0.25 * p^2 * VarB

carr_fb <- carr
carr_fb$var_total_raw[carr_fb$variable == num_code] <- VarA_neg

# A carrier row keyed on the rate name so the long rate row passes the
# carrier-key check; C1/C2 read the numerator/denominator ACS-code rows, not
# this placeholder, so its numeric fields are inert.
rate_carrier <- carr_fb[carr_fb$variable == num_code, , drop = FALSE][1, ]
rate_carrier$variable        <- "poverty_rate"
rate_carrier$estimand_family <- "derived_rate"
rate_carrier$est_total       <- NA_real_
rate_carrier$var_total_raw   <- 0
rate_carrier$est_mean        <- NA_real_
rate_carrier$var_mean_raw    <- 0
carr_fb <- bind_rows(carr_fb, rate_carrier)

# The long-format derived_rate row the formula will act on (built from a
# spatial_total template so all canonical columns and types are present).
rate_row <- weighted[weighted$variable == num_code, , drop = FALSE][1, ]
rate_row$variable              <- "poverty_rate"
rate_row$estimand_family       <- "derived_rate"
rate_row$estimate              <- NA_real_
rate_row$moe                   <- NA_real_
rate_row$weight_basis          <- "coverage"
rate_row$moe_formula_requested <- NA_character_
rate_row$moe_formula_effective <- NA_character_
rate_row$moe_fallback          <- NA
rate_row$moe_fallback_reason   <- "n/a"

weighted_fb <- bind_rows(weighted, rate_row)
attr(weighted_fb, "cacs_aggregation_carriers")  <- carr_fb
attr(weighted_fb, "cacs_schema_version")         <- "1.0"
attr(weighted_fb, "cacs_aggregation_provenance") <-
  attr(weighted, "cacs_aggregation_provenance")

# Confirm we have genuinely created a negative subset variance:
c(
  Var_A_set         = VarA_neg,
  scaled_Var_B      = p^2 * VarB,
  C1_inside_bracket = VarA_neg - p^2 * VarB   # < 0 by construction
)
        Var_A_set      scaled_Var_B C1_inside_bracket
         612.6206         2450.4825        -1837.8618

The bracket \mathrm{Var}(A) - (A/B)^2\,\mathrm{Var}(B) is negative, so C1 cannot produce a real margin. We now request proportion_subset for this rate through the locked formula argument and let the package decide:

propagated_fb <- cacs_propagate_moe(
  weighted_fb,
  formula = list(poverty_rate = "proportion_subset"),
  verbose = FALSE
)

fb_row <- propagated_fb |>
  filter(variable == "poverty_rate") |>
  select(variable, estimate, moe,
         moe_formula_requested, moe_formula_effective,
         moe_fallback, moe_fallback_reason)

fb_row
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  variable     estimate    moe moe_formula_requested moe_formula_effective
  <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>                 <chr>
1 poverty_rate    0.335 0.0246 proportion_subset     general_ratio_conservative
# ℹ 2 more variables: moe_fallback <lgl>, moe_fallback_reason <chr>

The status columns tell the whole story: moe_formula_requested is still "proportion_subset" (the request is preserved), but moe_formula_effective is "general_ratio_conservative", moe_fallback is TRUE, and moe_fallback_reason is "negative_variance". The fallback fired, and it is fully recorded — exactly the never-silent contract.

Step 3 — reproduce the C2 fallback value by hand

The recorded margin should be the C2 formula evaluated on the same inputs, M = z\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(A) + (A/B)^2\,\mathrm{Var}(B)}\,/\,|B|, and the estimate should be the proportion p = A/B:

hand_moe_C2 <- z * sqrt(VarA_neg + p^2 * VarB) / abs(B)

c(
  estimate_match = isTRUE(all.equal(p,           fb_row$estimate)),
  moe_match      = isTRUE(all.equal(hand_moe_C2, fb_row$moe)),
  moe_abs_diff   = abs(hand_moe_C2 - fb_row$moe)
)
estimate_match      moe_match   moe_abs_diff
             1              1              0

Both match exactly. The package’s fallback margin equals the hand-computed C2 root, and its estimate equals the proportion A/B. The run-level provenance attribute also counts the event:

attr(propagated_fb, "cacs_moe_provenance")$n_rows_fallback_c1_to_c2
[1] 1

One row took the C1 → C2 path, matching the single fallback we constructed.

To summarize the check: a Family A weighted root-sum-square reproduced by hand equals the package’s reported spatial_total margin to the floating-point floor on a partially-covered catchment; a deliberately negative C1 subset variance on the same catchment triggers the package’s never-silent C1 → C2 fallback, recorded as moe_formula_requested = "proportion_subset", moe_formula_effective = "general_ratio_conservative", moe_fallback = TRUE, and moe_fallback_reason = "negative_variance"; and the resulting C2 margin and the A/B estimate both reproduce by hand exactly. The formulas in this article and the arithmetic in the code are the same arithmetic, fallback included.

Where this sits

This article derived and verified the uncertainty half of the estimator. Its companions cover the spatial half and the rate catalogue, and the methodology overview ties all three together; each reuses the notation fixed in the overview.

  • The estimator overview, with the shared notation, the six-family table, and the four-family MOE summary this article expands: vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS"). This article is the derivation behind its margins-of-error section.
  • Spatial aggregation — the coverage and normalized mean weights this article carries margins through, the per-site intersection algorithm, and the point-estimate forms \widehat{Y}_s, \widehat{\bar X}_s, \widehat{R}_s: vignette("theory-spatial-aggregation", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_intersect_weight.
  • Derived rates — which of the curated rates are C1-eligible versus C2 by baseline policy, their ACS numerator/denominator pairs, and the carrier-lookup mechanics behind the ratio margins: vignette("theory-derived-rates", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_derive_rates.
  • Function reference — the four families, the C1 → C2 fallback, the full status-column contract, the five numerical guards, and the formula and level arguments are documented in ?cacs_propagate_moe; the SE ↔︎ MOE converters are ?cacs_se_to_moe and ?cacs_moe_to_se.

For the applied, run-it path that produces reporting tables with margins of error from these same fixtures, see vignette("getting-started", package = "catchmentACS") and vignette("alabama-tutorial", package = "catchmentACS").
